title: Objects that stick to the verb
goal: Attaching the direct object to the end of the verb — and watching the negative wrap stretch to hug both at once.
bekal: attaching object suffixes to past and present verbs
using double suffixes for sentences like "I'll send it to you"
making verbs that already carry a suffix negative

dialogs.title: حوار — موبايل ضايع
dialogs.intro: Budi has lost his phone. He calls Mona from a classmate's phone, and Mona tries to retrace his steps.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: استنى، ماتقلقش. آخر مرة شفته فين؟
lines.baca: istanna, mat’ala’sh. aakhir marra shuftu fēn?
lines.id: Wait, don't panic. Where did you last see it?
lines.literal: wait, don't-you-worry. last time you-saw-it where?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: مش فاكر. استعملته في القهوة الصبح.
lines.id: I don't remember. I used it at the café this morning.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: طيب، وبعد كده رحت فين؟ فكر بالراحة.
lines.baca: ṭayyib, wi ba‘d kida ruht fēn? fakkar bir-raaha.
lines.id: OK, and after that, where did you go? Think slowly.
lines.literal: OK, and after that you-went where? think with-the-ease.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.baca: rikibt il-mitro, wi ba‘dēn mishiit lil-ma‘had.
lines.id: I took the metro, and then I walked to the institute.
lines.literal: I-rode the-metro, and then I-walked to-the-institute.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: يمكن نسيته على الترابيزة. حاكلمهم دلوقتي.
lines.id: Maybe you left it on the table. I'll call them now.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: أنا عندي. ثانية واحدة، حاسألهم واكلمك.
lines.baca: ana ‘andi. sanya wahda, hasa’alhum wi akallimak.
lines.id: I've got it. One second, I'll ask them and call you back.
lines.literal: I have. second one, I-will-ask-them and I-call-you.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: God bless you. I'll be waiting.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: بودي! لقوه! الجرسون لقاه تحت الكرسي.
lines.baca: Buudi! la’uuh! ig-garsōn la’aah taht il-kursi.
lines.id: Budi! They found it! The waiter found it under the chair.
lines.literal: Budi! they-found-it! the-waiter he-found-it under the-chair.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Thank God! I can't believe it.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.id: They told me they'll keep it for you until tomorrow.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: لأ، حاروح دلوقتي. مش حاسيبه هناك.
lines.baca: la’, haruuh dilwa’ti. mish hasiibu hinaak.
lines.id: No, I'm going now. I'm not leaving it there.
lines.literal: no, I-will-go now. not I-will-leave-it there.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.baca: matinsaash tishkurhum. wi khud ba’shiish ma‘aak.
lines.id: Don't forget to thank them. And take a tip with you.
lines.literal: don't-you-forget you-thank-them. and take tip with-you.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: أكيد. شكراً يا منى، انتي أنقذتيني.
lines.baca: akiid. shukran ya Mona, inti an’aztiini.
lines.id: Of course. Thanks, Mona, you saved me.
lines.literal: sure. thanks O Mona, you you-saved-me.

notes: **Object suffixes are almost the same as possessive suffixes, except the first one.** For "my" the suffix is ـي (كتابي, my book); for "me" as an object it's **ـني** (شافني, he saw me). One letter makes the difference, and it's the only one that differs.
**English puts the object in a separate word; Egyptian Arabic glues it on.** شفته is one word meaning "I saw it". What takes English three words, Egyptian does in one.

**The word فاكر means "remembering", and it's an active participle, not a verb.** That's why its negative is مش فاكر, not the wrap. Its relatives: عارف (knowing), مصدق (believing), مستني (waiting) — all work the same way. Full treatment in unit seventeen.
**The word إن means "that", and the pronoun after it takes a suffix.** قالولي إنهم حيستنوه (they told me that they'd keep it). The forms: إني، إنك، إنه، إنها، إننا، إنكم، إنهم.

**The word بقشيش is a tip**, and it's a normal part of Egyptian life — for parking attendants, restroom attendants, people who help carry your bags, and anyone who helps you beyond their job. The amounts are small, but skipping it feels cold.

**The word ضاع means "got lost", and it works without a human doer.** الموبايل ضاع, not "I lost the phone". Egyptian prefers this pattern for accidents, a bit like English "my keys have gone missing".

grammars.title: Object suffixes
body: One table for every verb, and it works the same way in the past, the present, commands, and the future.
after: Notice that the suffixes are exactly the possessive suffixes from unit four, except the first row: **ـني for objects, ـي for possession**. So you're really learning one difference, not a whole new table.
For indirect objects — to whom — Egyptian uses لـ, which also sticks on: قالي *’alli* (he told me), قالها *’alha* (he told her), حاحكيلك *hahkiilak* (I'll tell you).

Both suffixes can appear at once, and the direct object always comes first: قالهالي *’alhaali* (he said it to me), إديهاله *iddiihaalu* (give it to him). You don't need to master this at A1, but you'll hear it a lot.

grammars.title: A negative that hugs the verb and its suffix
body: The rule hasn't changed since unit ten, but the effect is striking: the ـش goes on the very outside, after the object suffix.
after: Notice that the final vowel **lengthens** to hold the ـش, so شفته becomes ماشفتوش, with *u* turning into *uu*. It's the same thing that happened with the plural forms in unit ten.
The last two rows now make sense: عندي and فيه really do contain suffixes, and the wrap goes around the whole thing. No extra rule at all.

sections.title: Lost property, and how to deal with it

head: مصري
Say it
Meaning
rows: I lost it (lit. it got lost from me)

blocks.text: The sentence ضاع مني uses a typical pattern: the thing is the subject, and you're the one who loses out. Egyptian uses the same pattern for many accidents — وقع مني (it fell from me), اتكسر مني (it broke on me). It takes a little of the blame off your shoulders, and that's the point.

blocks.title: If you need the police
items: A police station is قسم *’ism*, and a loss report is محضر *mahḍar*. For insurance or a replacement passport, a محضر is almost always required.
The sentence: عايز أعمل محضر (I want to file a report). For an embassy: عايز أروح السفارة الإندونيسية (I want to go to the Indonesian embassy).
Emergency numbers in Egypt: police ١٢٢, ambulance ١٢٣, fire ١٨٠. Knowing them in Arabic numerals helps when you have to show them to someone.

blocks.text: Most verbs in this unit show up when calling and texting, so let's gather those sentences here.

The phrase مين معايا؟ literally means "who's with me?", and it's the standard way to ask who's calling. Answer simply with your name, no extras: أنا بودي. Egyptians rarely say "this is…" the way English speakers do.
